title: The Artificial Equilibrium: Alkalinity Enhancement as Geo-Mythopoesis
text:
Alkalinity enhancement, a methodology within oceanographic carbon capture, proposes accelerating the marine carbon cycle by adding alkaline materials (such as silicates or olivine) to counteract ocean acidification and increase $\text{CO}_2$ uptake efficiency. At its core, this endeavor represents an attempt to chemically manage a planetary buffer system that has evolved over billions of years.

The difficult connection arises when examining the chemical principle—the forced elevation of carbonate equilibrium through engineered intervention—against classical theories of narrative structure and dramatic resolution (mythopoesis). A natural ecosystem maintains a delicate, complex, and perpetually self-regulating balance; similarly, profound human narratives are understood to resolve tension only by imposing artificial stability or defining rigid structural boundaries. The endeavor forces an analytical parallel: both the ocean's buffer capacity and classical plot structures require enormous inputs of energy (whether through atmospheric $\text{CO}_2$ draw down or resolving a tragic conflict) simply to appear temporarily stable, creating the illusion of equilibrium where underlying stresses persist.

This intersection challenges environmental chemists to think like structuralists: how does adding an external stabilizing chemical agent alter not just the local water chemistry, but the entire biogeochemical 'narrative' of the deep sea? The implication is that geoengineering interventions are not merely physical processes; they constitute massive acts of planetary narrative revision, potentially sacrificing natural entropy and dynamic flux for a highly managed, human-defined stability that may itself breed entirely new, unexpected systemic vulnerabilities.
